dedupe_keys.name: durban warwick early morning market income losses of indigenous food crop vendors from the 2022 floods covid 19 and 2021 unrest

description: This case study looks at how a string of shocks hit the informal traders who sell indigenous food crops at Durban's Warwick Early Morning Market in South Africa. Researchers at Mangosuthu University of Technology surveyed 34 vendors about the 2022 Durban floods, the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2021 civil unrest. Eighty-eight percent had lost income because of the floods, 71 percent because of COVID-19 and 68 percent because of the unrest. Regression analysis found that lack of cold storage, together with exposure to the shocks, significantly predicted how much income vendors lost. The authors call for urban food governance that includes informal vendors and for investment in post-harvest infrastructure such as cold storage. The article is free to read and download as open access under CC BY in Frontiers in Nutrition (2025), with full text in Europe PMC. Coverage is one central market in Durban. Caveats: a small cross-sectional sample; results are self-reported; the facts here come from the abstract. Simulation uses: loss rates and the protective effect of cold storage for informal food distribution nodes in flood and compound-shock scenarios. Related records: the Toronto food system climate vulnerability assessment (case_study-toronto-food-system-climate-vulnerability-assessment) takes a city-wide view of similar risks in a high-income setting.
